clue.text: Auxiliary verbs function properly

definitions.meaning: the two commonest English helping verbs are 'be' and 'have', written together here
to work or act as one should, like a well-mannered child or a machine that runs right

explanation.surface: A grammar note that helping verbs do their job correctly.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is a pair of words run together: BE and HAVE, both auxiliary verbs in English.
explanation.definitionFit: Conducting oneself well or working correctly is the ordinary sense of the verb.

clue.text: Theatre choreographer packs in forerunner of foxtrot

indicators.note: the first two words contain, packed inside them, the run of letters wanted

explanation.surface: A stage choreographer squeezes the start of a foxtrot into a routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forerunner of foxtrot' looks like the letter F; in the NATO phonetic alphabet the code word before Foxtrot is the one wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: In the radio alphabet Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta come first, and the fifth code word immediately precedes Foxtrot.

clue.text: Luther oddly stops a German artist, one who cheats

indicators.note: the odd letters plug, or stop up, the artist's name like a cork in a bottle

parts.note: Albrecht Dürer was the great German Renaissance painter and engraver

indicators.note: take the letters in odd positions of Luther: first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: Martin Luther, behaving strangely, halts a German painter accused of cheating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stops' is the container signal: the odd letters plug the painter's name like a cork. 'Luther' and 'German' together suggest the Reformation, but the artist is Albrecht Dürer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is unfaithful to a spouse is said to cheat on them.

clue.text: E.g. Homer work, English poet's eye-opener

parts.note: Alexander Pope, the eighteenth-century English poet (who translated Homer)

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter, here of eye

explanation.surface: Homer's work as described by an English poet was a revelation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eye-opener' is split: 'opener' takes the first letter of 'eye'. Pope fits the surface well, as he translated the Iliad.
explanation.definitionFit: An epic poem, such as the Iliad or the Odyssey, is the kind of long heroic work Homer wrote.

clue.text: Top river reached, crossing another

parts.note: the Tees is a river in north-east England

indicators.note: the verb for reached lies across, i.e. around, the second river's letter

parts.note: to hit a target is to reach it
another river, abbreviated R

explanation.surface: An explorer reaches the top of one river after crossing a second.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' is the definition: a garment, not a summit.
explanation.definitionFit: A short-sleeved cotton garment worn on the upper body is a casual kind of top.

clue.text: Video of riveting broadcast that follows 11

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters of the three words are spread into a new order

explanation.surface: A riveting video is broadcast after another programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 across is the first half of Pope's line from An Essay on Criticism; this is the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: Pope's famous saying continues after the comma with this phrase, completing the quotation begun at 11.

clue.text: Erstwhile Catholic on drugs giving absolution

parts.note: erstwhile means former, written as ex
a drug user is said to be using

explanation.surface: A lapsed Catholic who takes drugs is being forgiven.
explanation.definitionFit: To pardon or let someone off a fault is to grant them absolution, a near synonym.

clue.text: Back university person who studies 22

parts.note: hind means rear or back, as in hind legs

explanation.surface: Someone supporting a university scholar who studies a subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is VEDA, the Vedas being the oldest scriptures of the faith.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of the religion whose oldest sacred texts are the Vedas would study them.

clue.text: Swerve round a large truck carrying a judge again

indicators.note: to turn round is to face the other way, so the word for swerve runs backwards

parts.note: to veer is to swerve
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

indicators.note: the vehicle carries, i.e. holds inside it, the second a

parts.note: a ute is a utility truck, an Australian pickup

explanation.surface: A driver swerves round a big lorry with a judge riding in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' turns the swerve word backwards and 'carrying' puts the second 'a' in the truck. A ute is the Australian name for a pickup truck.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess or appraise something a second time is to judge it once more.

clue.text: Dismiss small rough unstable fellows

parts.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

indicators.note: something unstable will not stay put, so the letters of rough shift around

parts.note: FF, a doubled F, abbreviates fellows

explanation.surface: Someone waves away a small gang of rough, shaky men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unstable' rearranges ROUGH into HRUGO.
explanation.definitionFit: To brush aside or disregard something with indifference is an idiom for dismissing it.

clue.text: Scrub part of church, not hotel

indicators.note: not here means without, so the letter for hotel is dropped

parts.note: the chancel is the part of a church around the altar
H is Hotel in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: An instruction to clean part of a church but leave the hotel alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrub' looks like cleaning; it is the informal sense of calling something off.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrub a plan informally means to call it off or abandon it.

clue.text: Corrupt hirsute Roman Pope's wise words

indicators.note: to corrupt is to spoil or distort, so the two words' letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A shaggy, crooked Roman Pope delivers a wise saying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pope' suggests a pontiff, but it is the poet Alexander Pope, author of the line.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a famous maxim from Alexander Pope's Essay on Criticism, so the poet's wise words.

clue.text: French author supports scary woman that's brought on board

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits below, so it comes second

parts.note: a gorgon is a frightening woman, after the Medusa myth
Émile Zola, the French novelist

explanation.surface: A French writer backs a frightening woman who is invited aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought on board' suggests a ship or a committee; the board is a cheese board.
explanation.definitionFit: This blue Italian cheese is something served on a cheese board after dinner.

clue.text: Yahoo loves taking over area in pub

indicators.note: the two zeros take the place of the letter for area, replacing it

parts.note: a bar is a pub
love is zero in tennis scoring, written O; two of them make OO

explanation.surface: An internet company's affection is spreading through a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yahoo' looks like the web company; it is the brutish Yahoos of Gulliver's Travels.
explanation.definitionFit: A yahoo is a coarse, uncouth person, after Swift's brutes in Gulliver's Travels.

clue.text: Top Jesuit retires to become a new soldier

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the whole string of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: a colour that becomes or suits you
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: The head Jesuit steps down to become a new soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retires' reverses SUIT + A + N + GI as one string; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: St Ignatius of Loyola founded the Society of Jesus and was its first Superior General.

clue.text: Tourist and cashier take in party briefly

indicators.note: the cashier encloses the shortened party, taking it in

parts.note: a bank teller is a cashier

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter of rave goes

parts.note: a rave is a party

explanation.surface: A tourist and a cashier attend a short party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts the party word short and 'take in' has the cashier enclose what remains; 'and' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A person on a journey or holiday is a traveller in the ordinary sense.

clue.text: Image Homer modified to describe bug

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so the rearranged letters go around the bug
modified means changed, so the letters of Homer are rearranged

parts.note: to tap a phone is to bug it

explanation.surface: Homer's picture was altered to show an insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'modified' shuffles the poet's name and 'to describe' wraps it around the bug, as one describes a circle round a point. 'bug' is the verb for eavesdropping, not an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure of speech that likens one thing to another is a kind of literary image.

clue.text: I gave Reg fluid for pain

definitions.note: used as a verb, to pain someone

indicators.note: fluid means not fixed, so the letters of the three words flow into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone handed Reg liquid to ease his discomfort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pain' is a verb here, to hurt or distress.
explanation.definitionFit: To distress or wrong someone is to cause them pain, a synonym for the verb.

clue.text: One's book

definitions.meaning: read as 'one is', in the sense of one plays a part or one performs
a book of the New Testament

explanation.surface: Something belonging to someone is a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' looks possessive; read it as 'one does' or 'one performs'.
explanation.definitionFit: The fifth book of the New Testament records the deeds of the Apostles.

clue.text: Standard reader's sorry

parts.note: par is the standard, as in up to par
a don is a university teacher, and a reader is a senior lecturer

explanation.surface: A standard textbook reader is apologetic.
explanation.walkthrough: A reader is a university rank in Britain, just below professor; a don is a university teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are used as an apology, or to ask someone to repeat what was said.

clue.text: Make weak old Peruvian head over most of a big town

parts.note: the Incas ruled Peru before the Spanish conquest

indicators.note: the head goes over, i.e. covers, the other letters by enclosing them

parts.note: pate is an old word for the head

indicators.note: most of means all but the last letter

parts.note: a city is a big town

explanation.surface: An ancient Peruvian chief holds sway over most of a large town and saps its strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' drops the town's last letter, and 'over' has the head cover the 'a' plus that remnant. Pate is an old word for the top of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: To disable or deprive of strength is to make someone weak.

clue.text: Pay for a spirit when lunch is taken?

definitions.meaning: to make amends for a wrong
read as two words, at one o'clock, a typical lunchtime

parts.note: tone means mood or spirit, as of a meeting

explanation.surface: A drink at lunchtime has to be paid for.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer split as AT ONE gives the lunchtime hour; the question mark flags this.
explanation.definitionFit: To make amends for a sin or wrong is to pay for it in a moral sense.

clue.text: Live dangerously, devouring religious books

definitions.note: a singular word for a collection of scriptures

indicators.note: the first two words devour, i.e. swallow up, the letters wanted

explanation.surface: Living on the edge while consuming sacred texts.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Hindu scriptures are collectively known by this Sanskrit word for knowledge.

clue.text: God left to skulk about

indicators.note: the verb for skulk goes about, i.e. around, the letter for left

parts.note: to mooch about is to loiter or skulk

explanation.surface: A deity departs only to lurk around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like departed but is just the letter L; 'about' has the skulking verb go round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Moloch was a Canaanite deity to whom children were said to be sacrificed.

clue.text: Pampered batting failure nurses sprained leg

parts.note: in cricket the batting side is in

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so the failure holds the twisted letters

parts.note: a dud is a failure

indicators.note: a sprained limb is twisted, so the letters of leg are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cricketer who failed with the bat looks after a sprained leg and is spoilt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sprained' twists the letters of 'leg' and 'nurses' holds them inside the failure. In cricket the side batting is 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pampered and spoilt by having every wish gratified.

clue.text: Relaxed about umpire ignoring first of extras

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means about

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving out, so a letter is removed from the umpire

parts.note: a referee is an umpire

indicators.note: the first letter of the word extras

explanation.surface: A calm cricket umpire paying no attention to the extras.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring' removes an E from REFEREE, leaving REFREE. Extras are runs not scored off the bat in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Free of worry or responsibility means relaxed in temperament.

clue.text: Standard northern exam baffles Mike

indicators.note: a baffle is a screen around something, so the exam encloses the letter

parts.note: an oral is a spoken exam
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A routine northern examination confuses a man called Mike.
explanation.definitionFit: Usual or typical, conforming to the standard.
